verdict.reasoning: Patient reports “a terrible headache… on the left side” and “yeah I guess it's throbbing… on that left side,” and that it is “worse when I move… if I lean forward, or like move my head or neck, yeah, headache gets worse.”

Patient says “I noticed some zig-zag lines in my vision a few minutes before the headache started,” and later confirms blurred vision in both eyes: Doctor: “both eyes, OK.” This is consistent with a visual aura with bilateral blurred vision.

Doctor asks about bright lights and patient answers “Yeah well I'm , wearing sunglasses right now. It's just, you know, the light's really hurting my eyes,” indicating photophobia and use of sunglasses.
Patient says “I just feel like I need to vomit” and later: Doctor: “Have you vomited at all?” Patient: “Yeah. I vomited twice.”
Doctor asks if the pain came on suddenly or was gradual, and patient replies “Don't know, really. It just happened,” showing onset course is unclear.

Patient: “I did have a similar headache a few weeks ago.” Doctor: “How long did it last for?” Patient: “Couple of days.” Patient describes taking “painkillers” and having “to go to bed and rest,” implying improvement with rest and painkillers.
Doctor states “this is the second migraine you've had in the space of a month,” indicating a second episode this month.

Patient denies multiple red-flag symptoms: Fever (“no I don't feel feverish”), rash (“No, I haven't noticed anything like that”), speech problems (“No”), arm/leg numbness or weakness (“No”), and balance/coordination issues (“No”).
Doctor asks about head injuries: “Have you had a fall recently, or been knocked on the head?” Patient responds “No.”
When asked “do you have any other medical history I should be aware of?” Patient answers “No, nothing,” and denies prior migraine diagnosis.
Patient states “I take the pill, Microgynon.” Doctor asks “how long have you been on that for?” Patient: “three months.” Doctor confirms it is “for contraception.”
Patient: “My mum, my mum has, has migraines… My mom has an underactive thyroid as well,” which is hypothyroidism.
Doctor asks: “any other problems with for example, the brain, or? Um you mentioned brain cancer. Any other family history of ?” Patient replies “No,” indicating no known family brain cancer.
Patient: “I work in the fashion industry,” and “Yeah it's really stressful, actually… managers like putting a lot of pressure on me to deliver.”
Patient says “I live on my own” and when asked about exercise: “Do you do much in the way of exercise?” Patient: “No.”
Doctor asks “do you smoke at all? and do you drink much in the way of alcohol?” Patient answers “No. No.” indicating nonsmoker and no alcohol use.
Doctor: “are you coping OK at the moment?” Patient: “Fine,” indicating they are coping okay.

Transcript shows visual phenomena before headache (zig-zag lines), unilateral throbbing headache, photophobia, nausea with two episodes of vomiting, recurrent episode, and denials of fever, focal deficits, speech/balance issues, and head injury. Doctor explicitly says “I wonder whether you may, uh may have a migraine… very classical.” No red-flag neurological signs are present.

Patient repeatedly expresses fear of brain cancer: “I've read… it could be a sign of brain cancer,” “My friend's mum… died of a brain tumor,” and worries about future and career. Doctor later reassures: “I'm reassured that you don't have anything more serious… such as… Brain cancer.”
Doctor advises: “some strong painkillers would be advisable. So, think about Paracetamol, or even Co-codamol… and some anti-inflammatories, such as Ibuprofen and Naproxen.”
Doctor: “I think keeping a headache diary would be quite important, uh to see exactly what's triggering these headaches,” which is advising a diary and trigger identification.
Doctor: “then we could have a discussion next time I see you next week, perhaps,” implying a follow-up review next week.

Doctor: “if your headaches were to become more persistent, then we could maybe think about giving you some medications that will stop your headaches from happening in the first place, something prophylactic medicines,” i.e., consider prophylactic therapy if persistent/frequent.

Doctor advises: “if your symptoms aren't getting better next two three days, or indeed they're getting worse… come back and see me… if your headache's getting worse, not responding to medications Or your um neck pain is getting worse, or you develop any weakness in your arms and legs, or your vision, then I want you to come back and see me straight away,” matching the stated safety-net advice.
